title: Exposure to Political Violence and Post-Traumatic Stress Among Palestinian Youth: The Role of Individual and Socio-Environmental Factors
abstract: Abstract The present study examined the relationship between Palestinian adolescents’ exposure to political violence (EPV) and post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS), as well as the potential moderating effects of individual and socio-environmental factors on this relationship. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2,721 Palestinian adolescents aged 12–19 ( M = 16.01, SD = 0.94; 58% girls) and one of their parents, using self-report questionnaires. Data collection was conducted between October 2010 and January 2011. Results indicated that higher levels of EPV were significantly associated with greater PTSS. Although boys reported higher exposure to political violence than girls, girls exhibited more severe PTSS. Older adolescent boys reported higher levels of exposure than younger boys, whereas older adolescent girls reported lower levels of exposure than younger girls. Gender (being male) moderates the impact of exposure to political violence on PTSS, in particular in late adolescence (17–19 years). Family social support, but not peer support or perceived social capital, was negatively associated with PTSS. No moderating effects were found for social support or perceived social capital. These findings underscore the importance of prevention efforts aimed at reducing adolescents’ exposure to political violence and enhancing their protection. Furthermore, they emphasize the need for targeted interventions that strengthen family support systems for adolescents at heightened risk, particularly girls and older male youth.
